1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6.name: Four Knights Game
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6.background: Popular among the Open Games in the nineteenth century, the Four Knights had lost ground by the First World War, and it saw a renaissance in the 1990s, since when grandmasters have played it again.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the second knight and keeps the position symmetrical and solid. Black takes no risks, but White decides the character of the game, which tends to be quiet and drawish, and Black has little scope to unbalance it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Bb4.name: Three Knights Opening
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Bb4.strategy: Develops the bishop and hits the knight, but it is early: the d2 pawn still stands behind the knight, so there is no pin, and White can jump to d5, attacking the bishop and gaining time.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6.name: Three Knights Opening: Steinitz Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the bishop to g7, aiming it down the long diagonal, but it is slow: White can open the centre before Black is ready, and Black has to catch up in development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 f5.name: Three Knights Opening: Winawer Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 f5.strategy: Gambits the f-pawn to hit e4, but it weakens Black's own king and White can simply take the pawn. Black has little to show for the sacrifice.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nd5.strategy: Answers the early bishop at once: the knight jumps to d5 and attacks it. Black has to spend time on the bishop while White's knight stands in the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bb5.strategy: Mirrors Black's bishop and attacks the c6 knight that guards e5. A balanced set-up in which both sides pressure the other's knight; it develops soundly but gives White little to play for.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bc4.strategy: Develops towards f7 and prepares castling, a natural set-up aimed at that square. It leaves Black's bishop on b4, where it pins the c3 knight and can trade itself for it, so the game stays balanced without White choosing a plan.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nd5 Nf6.name: Three Knights Opening: Schlechter Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nd5 Nf6.strategy: Develops with a threat: the knight attacks the e4 pawn, which lost its guard when the c3 knight left, and challenges the knight on d5. White can still trade on b4 or f6 first.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nd5 Ba5.strategy: The usual retreat: the bishop keeps its pin along the diagonal, so the d2 pawn cannot move, and Black avoids a trade on b4. White still leads in development and the knight on d5 stands well, but Black stays solid.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nd5 Bc5.strategy: Moves the bishop out of danger and eyes f2, but puts it where a pawn can hit it. White takes on e5, and after the recapture the pawn on d4 attacks bishop and knight together; the pieces trade off level, with White ahead in development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6 4.d4.strategy: Strikes in the centre while Black's fianchetto is still unfinished. The e5 pawn is attacked twice and defended once, so Black has to resolve the tension at once, and White's pieces come out with more space.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Bc4.strategy: Develops with an eye on f7 and prepares castling, a calm choice that leaves Black time to finish the fianchetto. White passes up the immediate strike in the centre and keeps it for later.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Bb5.strategy: Puts the bishop on the diagonal that attacks the c6 knight, the guard of e5. The pressure is mild, since the knight is also covered by pawns, and Black simply continues with the fianchetto: a modest, flexible set-up.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6 4.d4 exd4.strategy: Trades the attacked pawn rather than defending it passively, and keeps the c6 knight pressing on d4. The price is time: White recaptures with a lead in development, and Black has to catch up with the fianchetto.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6 4.d4 Bg7.strategy: Finishes the fianchetto and adds a second guard to e5, which White attacks twice. Black gives up the quick pawn trade, so White decides how the tension in the centre is resolved and keeps the extra space.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6 4.d4 d6.strategy: Supports e5 with a pawn, but White takes on e5 and the queens come off with check on d8: Black either recaptures with the king and loses the right to castle, or gives up the e5 pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6 4.d4 exd4 5.N.name: Three Knights Opening: Steinitz-Rosenthal Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6 4.d4 exd4 5.N.strategy: Plants the knight on an outpost Black's pawns cannot easily challenge: the e-pawn is gone and the c-pawn is blocked by its own knight. From d5 it eyes c7 and f6, and the d4 pawn is still to be won back, so White keeps the initiative.

Recaptures the pawn with the knight and offers to trade off the c6 knight. If Black takes on d4, the queen recaptures and hits the h8 rook along the long diagonal, so Black has to meet that threat at once. White gets the freer development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6 4.d4 exd4 5.Q.strategy: Recaptures with the queen, but the knight on c6 takes it: White loses the queen for a knight.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bb5.strategy: Attacks the knight that guards e5 and asks Black to react. Unlike in the Ruy Lopez, the c3 knight takes the square from White's c-pawn, so there is no broad pawn centre to build, and the game stays even and manoeuvring rather than sharp.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3.name: Four Knights Game: Glek System
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3.background: A modern try advocated by Igor Glek.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, castle and build up slowly. It leads to a less drawish game than most of the Four Knights, but Black can equalise with a sound central strike.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4.name: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4.background: With 4.Bb5, one of the two most common continuations of the Four Knights Game.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4.strategy: Opens the centre at once: White removes Black's e-pawn and develops with space and open lines, with the knight already on c3. It is more direct than the quiet lines, but Black develops easily.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.a3.name: Four Knights Game: Gunsberg Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.a3.background: A specialty of the Polish grandmaster Paweł Blehm.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.a3.strategy: A waiting move: it takes b4 from Black's bishop and passes the turn, hoping for a Four Knights with colours reversed. It develops nothing, so Black can simply take the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nd5.name: Four Knights Game: Naroditsky Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nd5.background: A blitz favourite of Daniel Naroditsky. After his death Hikaru Nakamura played it in memoriam against Magnus Carlsen and called for the line to be known by his name.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nd5.strategy: Leaves the e4 pawn undefended on purpose. A Black knight that grabs it wins a pawn or two, but White gets an active position with traps for the unwary; calm development is the safer way to meet it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nxe5.name: Four Knights Game: Halloween Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nxe5.background: In 1888 Oskar Cordel reported that Leipzig club players used the gambit to dangerous effect; their name for it, the Müller–Schulze Gambit, was a joke in German and did not refer to any real players. The modern name was given by the German player Steffen Jakob, who compared the shock of facing it when prepared for a boring Four Knights to being frightened by a Halloween mask.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nxe5.strategy: Gives a knight for a pawn in the hope of a lead in development and a pawn centre that drives Black's knights back. Black simply takes the knight, keeps the extra piece and can return it on good terms, so the compensation is not enough.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.a3 d6.strategy: A solid reply that guards e5 and opens the c8 bishop's diagonal, keeping the position symmetrical. It is a little passive: claiming the centre with a pawn is the more ambitious way to punish the waiting move.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.a3 d5.strategy: Strikes in the centre at once: White's a-pawn move has done nothing for the middle, so Black challenges the e4 pawn and fights for space with a pawn. Black reaches a comfortable, active game without weaknesses, the most direct answer to a waiting move.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.a3 Be7.strategy: Develops the bishop modestly and prepares to castle: a safe, solid set-up with no weaknesses. It leaves the centre to White, who can expand or keep things quiet, so Black plays for equality rather than the initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.a3 d6 5.h3.name: Four Knights Game: Gunsberg Variation, Provincial Opening
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.a3 d6 5.h3.strategy: A second waiting move, this time taking g4 from Black's bishop so that a pin on the f3 knight never comes. White keeps a flexible, solid set-up, but two prophylactic moves in a row leave Black free to develop as it likes.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.a3 d6 5.d4.strategy: Opens the centre and fights for space: White challenges the e5 pawn before Black has finished developing. The game becomes open and active, with White the one deciding how the centre is exchanged and the pieces getting more room.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.a3 d6 5.Bb.strategy: Brings the bishop out against the c6 knight, which guards e5, and so adds indirect pressure on the centre. Black can answer calmly with a solid set-up and the game stays level; White keeps the option of exchanging on c6 and a flexible development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.a3 d6 5.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop and castle, a flexible set-up that does not commit the centre. The bishop presses on the long diagonal from a distance, but White concedes space and lets Black occupy the centre freely.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4.name: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation Accepted
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4.strategy: Takes the pawn with tempo, as the capture attacks the c3 knight at once. The centre opens and White has to recover the pawn or move the knight, while Black accepts an open game with no weaknesses of its own.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 Bb4.strategy: Pins the c3 knight against the king, so that e4 loses its defender and Black threatens to take it. The cost is the e5 pawn, which is attacked twice and defended once: White can simply take it, and Black has to prove that the pin and the pressure on e4 pay for it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 d6.strategy: Defends e5 with a pawn and holds the centre together instead of opening it with ...exd4. The price is passivity: White keeps the space and decides when to open the centre, while Black has fewer active pieces.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 Bb4 5.N.name: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation, Krause Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 Bb4 5.N.strategy: Wins the e5 pawn, with the knight supported by the d4 pawn. It is a real gambit all the same: the pinned c3 knight leaves e4 short of defenders, so White takes the pawn at the price of quick counterplay against the centre and the exposed knights.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 Bb4 5.d.strategy: Drives the c6 knight away with a gain of space and leaves the e5 pawn undefended. The fight moves from the pawn to the centre: White has more room, Black has the pin on c3 and the loose e4 pawn to work with.

Takes the pawn and hits the f6 knight, but gives up the pawn centre, and ...Nxe4 regains the pawn at once with an attack on the pinned c3 knight. White has to untangle the pin, so the extra pawn buys little.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 Bb4 5.d.name: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation, Oxford Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 Bb4 5.d.strategy: Moves the attacked knight to the centre, where the e5 pawn guards it and where it eyes f3 and c2. Black gives up the e5 pawn for this, which White can take, and relies on the pin and the pressure on e4 and f3 for compensation.

Retreats the attacked knight and keeps all the pieces in play. Black lets the e5 pawn go, but the pinned c3 knight cannot defend e4, so ...Nxe4 is a standing threat that White has to take into account.

Trades the pinning bishop for the c3 knight to double White's pawns, and only then saves the attacked knight. Black gives up the pin and the bishop pair, and White's gains are the e5 pawn and the open b-file: sound but second-rate.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 Bb4 5.N.name: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation, Krause Gambit, Leonhardt Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 Bb4 5.N.strategy: Attacks the e5 knight a second time, so that the c6 knight and the queen together outweigh the d4 pawn that guards it, and brings the queen to the e-file. White cannot keep the extra pawn without finding more support for the knight.

A counterstroke: the knight takes the e4 pawn, which the pinned c3 knight cannot defend, and attacks that knight at once. Material is level again, but both sides' pieces are exposed and the king stays in the centre in a sharp game.
Castles and leaves the pawn for now, relying on the pin and the pressure on e4 to pay for it. Black's king is safe, but with no immediate threat White is free to consolidate and keep the extra pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: Recovers the pawn and puts the knight on a central square, defended by the queen, from where it eyes c6. White gets the open game it wanted, with simple development and the chance to trade on c6 and damage Black's pawn structure.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation, Belgrade Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..background: The first recorded game in this line was played between Kurt Richter and Albert Becker in Berlin in 1938. The association with Belgrade comes from the 1945 Belgrade championship, where it was played by Mihailo Trajkovic against Miroslav Radojcic.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: Sidesteps the attack by jumping forward and offers the e4 pawn in return for quick piece play. Black has several sound ways to take or decline and, with accurate play, equalises, so White gets practical chances at the price of a pawn.
Counterattacks the f6 knight but ignores the attack on the c3 knight: Black takes it with ...dxc3 and, after the trade on f6, is a pawn up with White's c-pawns doubled and one of them hanging.
Takes the offered pawn and keeps it for now, a sharp way to meet the gambit. Black asks White to show real compensation, since White's lead in development is all there is to pay for the pawn.
A quiet developing move that avoids the complications of the gambit and prepares castling. Black declines the e4 pawn and lets White regain the d4 pawn, but comes out with the healthier position.

The more testing reply: the knight attacks the d5 knight, which only the e4 pawn defends, and eyes c2, and the bishop on f8 protects it. Black keeps the extra pawn, but the game becomes tactical and White's lead in development counts.

Pins the e4 knight to the king and attacks it, with nothing yet defending it, while the d5 knight adds pressure around c7. Black has to defend at once and accurately; the move is the sharpest test of the pawn grab.
Develops at once, and the d5 knight eyes c7 and e7. White is a pawn down and plays for speed; Black has to find a safe, useful square for the loose e4 knight without losing time.

Attacks the e4 knight with the bishop and keeps the queen free, rather than pinning it. Black has several ways to hold the extra pawn, but White gets open lines for its pieces and quick development in return.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation, Belgrade Gambit, Modern Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: Defends the pinned knight with a pawn and so keeps the extra pawn. The price is a weakened kingside and an open diagonal from the king, and the pin is still there, so Black has to meet White's piece play with care.
Attacks the queen, but the e4 knight is pinned and loose: White simply takes it with check, Qxe4+, and the pawn on d3 does not help. Black loses a knight for nothing.
Defends the pinned knight with the queen, but the queen steps into the d5 knight's reach: Nxe7 wins it, and after the recapture the e4 knight falls too.

Pins the c3 knight and with it the defence of e4, while the c6 knight attacks the d4 knight, which only the queen guards. White cannot calmly defend the pawn and usually trades on c6 first. A natural main line that leaves Black with a sound, flexible game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..name: Four Knights Game: Scotch Variation, Schmid Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5..strategy: A temporary knight sacrifice: when White takes on e4, the queen pins that knight to the king and the c6 knight attacks the d4 knight, so Black wins the piece back. Material comes out equal in an open, unbalanced position that asks Black to know the follow-up.

A less committal alternative to the pin: the bishop hits the d4 knight, while the c3 knight is not pinned and e4 stays safe, so White can complete its development in peace. Black is active and the game stays level.

Trades the knights and lets the queen recapture in the centre, where it is active and not easily harassed. Black removes its own best-placed knight and wins nothing for it, which gives White the more comfortable game.

Trades off the knight that attacks d4, with tempo, since the capture also attacks the queen. White removes the target before the bishop defends e4 and forces Black to double the c-pawns, a structural concession that ...d5 can later repair.
Defends e4 but blocks the queen's protection of the d4 knight: ...Nxd4 wins the knight for nothing, since nothing on the board can recapture.
Breaks the pin on the c3 knight but leaves the d4 knight short of protection, since the bishop now blocks the queen: ...Nxd4 wins a piece.
Recaptures towards the centre and keeps the queens on, which the other recapture would not. The doubled c-pawns are a weakness, but Black gets an open b-file and can undouble them with ...d5.

Recaptures with the d-pawn, which opens the d-file and invites the queen trade: Qxd8+ forces the king to recapture and costs Black its castling rights. The structure is healthier than after bxc6, but the king's position is not.

Takes the c3 knight with check first, which doubles White's pawns after bxc3. Black still has to recapture on c6, so its own pawns double, and Black has parted with the bishop for a knight; the structures mirror each other.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 d5.strategy: Strikes at the centre at once: e4 is attacked by the d-pawn and the f6 knight and defended only by the c3 knight, so White has to resolve the tension. Black claims a share of the centre and reaches an equal game, which takes the sting out of the fianchetto plan.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop with an eye on f2 and keeps the centre flexible. Black does not strike at once: the fianchetto is a slower plan, and sound development is enough to equalise.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 Nxe4.strategy: A speculative piece sacrifice: Black gives a knight for a pawn. After White takes, ...d5 attacks the e4 knight, but it can step back, so Black has only a pawn and a few open lines for the piece.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 d5 5.ex.strategy: Resolves the tension by capturing, since e4 is attacked twice and defended once. The centre opens before the bishop reaches g2, and White prepares to use the long diagonal later in a game of quick development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 d5 5.Bg.strategy: Develops the bishop, but the f3 knight blocks its diagonal, so e4 is attacked twice and defended once. After ...dxe4 the pawn also attacks the knight, and White cannot recapture on e4 without dropping a piece.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 d5 5.d3.strategy: Supports the e4 pawn, so a trade on e4 leads to a queen exchange in which the king recaptures and White gives up castling. The position stays level and safe, but White gives up any hope of an initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.g3 d5 5.ex.strategy: Recaptures with the knight, which settles on a central square and attacks the c3 knight. Black's pieces become active, the d-pawn is gone from the centre, and Black has to be ready to meet the pressure White builds with the fianchetto.
Hangs the queen: the knight on c3 takes it at once, and Black gets only a knight in return.
Goes for the d5 pawn and the c2 square, but leaves the e5 pawn without a defender, so Nxe5 wins it. The knight is also offside on b4, and Black has spent a tempo to end up a pawn down.

Puts the bishop on the long diagonal, the point of the g3 set-up, behind the f3 knight, and prepares castling. White accepts a quiet game and pressure on the centre and the queenside from a distance, instead of occupying it.
Trades off Black's centralised knight and makes the queen recapture in the middle. The game stays even and simple: White gives up the c3 knight's grip on d5, and Black's queen comes out early.

Develops with pressure on the d5 knight, but the knight trade on c3 is easy for Black to take. If White recaptures with the d-pawn, the queens come off with check and the king loses castling; the b-pawn recapture doubles White's pawns.

Trades off White's knight on c3. Either recapture doubles White's c-pawns, though it opens the b-file or the d-file for White. Black simplifies and eases the game, at the price of letting the g2 bishop work freely.
Retreats instead of exchanging, keeps every piece and leaves White's pawns undoubled. The knight is less active on b6 and White castles at leisure, but Black's position is solid.

Adds a defender to the d5 knight and develops the bishop, which can recapture on d5 and then line up against the f3 knight on the long diagonal. It commits the bishop early, and Black must be ready for the exchange on d5.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nxe5 Nxe5.strategy: Takes the knight: Black is a piece up for a pawn and White's compensation is a lead in development. Accepting is the critical reply, since it puts the extra material to the test and leaves White to prove the attack.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nxe5 Nxe4.strategy: Takes the e4 pawn at once instead of the piece, which levels the material, but White keeps the better game: Qh5 threatens mate on f7 and Black has to defend. Black gives up the extra piece for nothing.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nxe5 Bc5.strategy: Declines the knight without winning anything back, so Black stays a pawn down and hopes quick development and the bishop's aim at f2 make up for it. White can simply take on c6 and keep the pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nxe5 Nxe5.strategy: The point of the gambit: the pawn attacks the e5 knight with tempo and White builds a broad centre with the e-pawn. White hopes to drive the black knights back and make the lead in development count before Black can untangle.
Hits the knight with a pawn but develops nothing and loosens the diagonal to the king: Black simply moves the knight and keeps the extra piece, with White no nearer to compensation.
Slow and quiet: with no pawn attacking the e5 knight, Black consolidates and finishes development. The central pawn play that was to pay for the piece is gone.

Goes back to c6, where it attacks the d4 pawn and stays in the centre. It keeps the extra piece and leaves Black with more good answers to White's space-gaining pawn moves than the retreat to the edge.

Retreats to g6, out of the pawn's reach, and keeps the piece. The knight is awkwardly placed and the f6 knight can be chased back, so Black spends time to hold the material, with a solid game if it consolidates.

Takes the e4 pawn and gives the piece back: after Nxe4 the e5 knight is still attacked and the material is level. White keeps the bigger centre and the lead in development, so Black gives up the point of accepting the gambit.

Chases the c6 knight again with a pawn, gaining space at the cost of time. White keeps the gambit going and plays for speed instead of material, but the pawn on d5 is also a target and Black has good ways to meet the attack.
Adds a defender to d4 and develops, so White keeps the pawn centre without further commitment. It makes no threat, though, and Black gets time to untangle and make use of the extra piece.
Develops quietly and prepares castling, with d4 still guarded by the queen and e4 by the knight. White gives up the speed that the gambit lives on, and Black gets time to consolidate.

Jumps back to e5 and keeps the piece, but the knight can be chased again and White's central pawns gain more space with each move. Black's pieces are pushed about and White's attack is dangerous in practice, so the defence has to be exact.

Pins the c3 knight against the king and meets the capture on c6 with a counter-attack on e4, so Black regains the material and keeps the more active pieces. White's attack runs out of steam, and the game leans to Black.

Retreats the knight to its home square instead of into the pawns' grip, keeping the extra piece but giving back all the time spent on it. White gains space and tempi, and Black has to untangle without falling to the attack.

Drives the f6 knight back with the pawn, gaining space and time. White's central pawns and lead in development are the compensation for the piece; if Black consolidates safely, White is simply a piece down.

Aims to chase the g6 knight from its post with a rook-pawn advance and make Black lose more time. It commits a pawn on the wing, though, and does nothing for development or the central pawns, so Black keeps a comfortable extra piece.
Develops the bishop to its most active diagonal, eyeing f7, with e4 guarded by the knight and d4 by the queen. Nothing is threatened, though, and Black can consolidate the extra piece.

Retreats all the way home and keeps the extra piece, the usual way to hold the material. It undoes Black's development, so White's pawns dominate the centre and Black has to catch up without falling into tactics, but with accurate play the extra piece tells; Black may also return it for a calmer game.

Pins the c3 knight and hands back the extra piece on Black's terms: after exf6 the queen recaptures with a hit on d4, the material is level, and Black has the lead in development and the pressure in the centre.
